balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Aviva plc: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Aviva plc: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units (pence).

For Aviva plc: a 76-for-100 share consolidation took effect in 2022 (following the sale of several international businesses and a capital return), so per-share figures before and after 2022 are not directly comparable without adjustment -- a step in EPS/DPS around that date is a share-count mechanic, not a profit or dividend-policy change. The July 2025 Direct Line Group acquisition also increased shares outstanding, diluting per-share metrics independent of underlying earnings growth.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt
  • Don't compare pre-2022 and post-2022 per-share levels without rebasing for the consolidation

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Aviva plc: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Aviva plc: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Aviva plc: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Aviva plc: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Aviva plc: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Aviva plc: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

totalIncome.title: Total income
totalIncome.content:
Net interest income plus fees and other operating income.

For Aviva plc: the top line for a financial; revenue in the ordinary sense does not apply.

What to watch:

  • Income growth versus cost growth

underlyingProfit.title: Underlying operating profit & operating EPS
underlyingProfit.content:
Group adjusted (underlying) operating profit strips out short-term investment-market volatility, one-off restructuring and M&A costs from statutory IFRS profit; operating EPS is the per-share version management guides to and the market prices off.

For Aviva plc: statutory net income swings with investment markets and acquisition accounting (e.g. Direct Line integration costs), so the board's own targets -- and this dashboard's EPS-vs-adjusted-EPS comparison -- are set against this line, not the IFRS net income chart above. FY2025 underlying profit of £2,203m (+25% YoY) beat the 2026 £2.0bn target a year early.

What to watch:

  • Growth in underlying profit versus statutory net income (the gap is the adjustment quality)
  • Operating EPS growth against the 11% 2025-28 CAGR target
  • Only populated FY2024 onward in the extracted data -- no pre-2024 trend to compare against

solvencyRatio.title: Solvency II shareholder cover ratio
solvencyRatio.content:
The Solvency II cover ratio is eligible own funds divided by the regulatory Solvency Capital Requirement -- the primary capital-adequacy signal for a European insurer, analogous to a bank's CET1 ratio.

For Aviva plc: management targets a cover ratio comfortably above 100%, typically guiding to a working range in the 160-180%+ area; it absorbs dividends, buybacks and acquisition financing (the ratio fell from 180% at FY2025 to 171% at Q1 2026 after the final dividend, a £350m buyback and the end of Tier 2 debt grandfathering).

What to watch:

  • A sustained fall toward the regulatory minimum, which would constrain the dividend/buyback capacity this stock is bought for
  • Only two data points (FY2022: 212%, FY2023: 207%) are captured in the CSV -- treat this chart as a historical snapshot, not a live trend; more recent ratios are in management commentary only

premium.title: Gross written premium & net earned premium
premium.content:
Gross written premium (GWP) is total premium income before reinsurance ceded; net earned premium (NEP) is GWP net of reinsurance and earned over the policy period -- the standard scale measures for general-insurance underwriting under the old IFRS 4 basis.

For Aviva plc: this series ends at FY2022 because IFRS 17 (effective FY2023) replaced GWP/NEP-based disclosure with the Insurance Service Result shown in the next chart -- the drop to zero is a reporting-basis change, not a collapse in underwriting volume. The 2022 divestment of the French, Polish, Italian and other international businesses also shrank the group's premium base before the accounting change.

What to watch:

  • Pre-2023 only: GWP/NEP growth as a proxy for underwriting scale
  • Post-2023: use the Insurance Service Result chart instead

insuranceServiceResult.title: Insurance service result (IFRS 17)
insuranceServiceResult.content:
Under IFRS 17, the insurance service result is the underwriting profit on insurance contracts (premium revenue less claims, expenses and the release of risk-adjustment and contractual-service-margin reserves) -- it replaces the old GWP/NEP/combined-ratio disclosure as the headline underwriting line.

For Aviva plc: this is populated from FY2022 (restated comparative) onward and is the measure to use for underwriting trend post transition; the July 2025 Direct Line Group acquisition (>20% of UK motor) should show up here as a step-change in scale from FY2025/H1 FY2026 onward, consolidated into UK&I General Insurance Personal Lines.

What to watch:

  • Step-change from FY2025/H1 FY2026 as Direct Line consolidates
  • Not comparable level-for-level with pre-2023 GWP/NEP -- different accounting basis, not a smaller business
